titre: Tordesillas (1494): A Negotiated Line, Not a Papal Decree
accroche: On June 7, 1494, Spain and Portugal set the line dividing them at 370 leagues from Cape Verde. The pope's bull a year earlier said 100.
contenu_vulgarise:
We often read that the pope divided the world between Spain and Portugal. In 1493, he did designate a boundary. But it is not the one in the Treaty of Tordesillas, concluded the following year between the two crowns.

## A First Line, Papal, Judged Too Close

In the bull *Inter caetera* of 1493, Pope Alexander VI designates as the eastern boundary of the Spanish zone a meridian located one hundred leagues west of the Azores or the Cape Verde Islands. Portugal feels wronged. It wants another meridian, farther west, halfway between the Cape Verde Islands and the lands discovered by Columbus.

## Nearly Ten Months of Negotiation Between Crowns

Talks begin in Barcelona around mid-August 1493. In November, an embassy led by Garcia de Carvajal and Pedro de Ayala is sent to the Portuguese court; it comes to nothing. In March 1494, the Portuguese commissioners Ruy de Sousa, João de Sousa and Ayres de Almada deal directly with the Spanish sovereigns, at Medina del Campo. On June 7, 1494, at Tordesillas, near Valladolid, three Spanish representatives conclude the treaty with Portugal's plenipotentiaries.

The text provides for a line drawn straight, from pole to pole, from the Arctic pole to the Antarctic pole, three hundred seventy leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands. The king and queen of Spain ratify on July 2, 1494, the king of Portugal on September 5. The pope is not the author of the agreement: the sovereigns beg him to be pleased to confirm and approve it, and to have bulls issued to that effect.

## A Line No One Could Measure

The treaty does not say from which Cape Verde island to start. According to the introduction by the American editor of the text, Frances Davenport, Portugal claimed, as its interests dictated, now one, now another. The number of leagues that make up a degree was also debated. For lack of any means of determining the meridian's position at the time, the treaty gave rise to new disagreements, and its interpretation, Davenport writes, remained disputed into the modern era.

Moving the line had concrete consequences. UNESCO, which inscribed the treaty in its Memory of the World register in 2007, on a joint nomination by Portugal and Spain, writes that the shift of the demarcation line led to the birth of Brazil, whose eastern tip fell within the Portuguese zone.

## What Remains of the Phrase

The phrase “the pope divided the world” retains a kernel of truth: a bull did set a first boundary, at one hundred leagues. The line that bears the name of Tordesillas is another one, obtained between two states, which the pope was asked to confirm.

repere.texte: The 1493 bull *Inter caetera* set the boundary at one hundred leagues west of the Azores or the Cape Verde Islands. The Treaty of Tordesillas, concluded on June 7, 1494 between Spain and Portugal, moves it to three hundred seventy leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands.
repere.source: Davenport, *European Treaties Bearing on the History of the United States to 1648* (1917), Document 9, introduction and treaty of June 7, 1494

carte.punch: The pope had drawn the line at 100 leagues. The Treaty of Tordesillas places it at 370, by negotiation.
carte.idee: In 1493, the bull *Inter caetera* sets a boundary one hundred leagues west of Cape Verde. Portugal feels wronged. After nearly ten months of talks between crowns, the treaty of June 7, 1494 moves it to 370 leagues. The pope is asked to confirm it.

quiz.question: Who sets the 370-league line of the Treaty of Tordesillas?
choix: Pope Alexander VI, through the bull *Inter caetera* issued in 1493
A commission of cartographers appointed by the pope, which measures the line in 1494
The king of Portugal alone, who imposes it on Spain after the failure of the 1493 embassy
The representatives of the crowns of Spain and Portugal, after months of negotiation
quiz.explication: The treaty is negotiated and then concluded between the representatives of the two crowns, who then ask the pope to confirm it. The 1493 bull, by contrast, set a boundary at one hundred leagues, which Portugal judged too close, and the text mentions neither a pontifical commission nor a decision by a single king.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why did Portugal contest the boundary set by the 1493 bull *Inter caetera*?
choix: It judged the one-hundred-league line too close and wanted one farther west
It refused any boundary drawn by the pope, whatever it was
It demanded a boundary drawn east to west rather than north to south
It challenged Pope Alexander VI's authority over this dispute
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text says that Portugal feels wronged by the line at one hundred leagues and wants a meridian farther west, halfway between Cape Verde and the lands discovered by Columbus.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where do the Portuguese commissioners deal directly with the Spanish sovereigns, in March 1494?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text places these March 1494 talks at Medina del Campo, before the treaty was concluded at Tordesillas on June 7 of the same year.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What remains uncertain in the text of the Treaty of Tordesillas itself, according to Frances Davenport?
choix: The exact date of its signing
Which Cape Verde island serves as the line's starting point
The total number of leagues separating the two zones
The identity of the signatory sovereigns
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Davenport notes that the treaty does not specify which Cape Verde island to start from, which Portugal claimed now one way, now another, according to its interests.
